newsitem.title: UK: UK Hague's appointments hint at rightward shift.
newsitem.headline: UK Hague's appointments hint at rightward shift.

text.p: Britain's new opposition leader William Hague on Friday made the first appointments to his shadow cabinet and signalled that he may be shifting his demoralised party further to the political right.
He gave key posts to three of his right wing rivals in the leadership election and appointed former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's right hand man -- Cecil Parkinson -- as party chairman.

The most important acceptance was that of John Redwood, who carried the support of the party's Eurosceptics through two rounds of the leadership vote but then allied with Hague's moderate rival Kenneth Clarke during the final round of the leadership race.
Redwood evidently decided to bury his pride and accept the job of shadow trade and industry secretary.

"He asked me to do a senior job in the shadow cabinet (and) it would be churlish to refuse. We must put the interests of the party first and so I'm doing it for the sake of party unity and so that I can work hard for the team," said Redwood.
"The party has made its decision about who is the leader and it's now the job of all of us to get behind the leader and to help him when he asks."

Peter Lilley and Michael Howard will respectively become shadow finance and foreign affairs spokesmen while Stephen Dorrell -- who quit the leadership race before the first ballot -- will become shadow education and employment secretary.
There was no job for Clarke. The pro-European former Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) had made clear he would not serve on the opposition front benches unless he won the leadership.

Hague, who at 36 is the Conservative's youngest leader for some 200 years, won Thatcher's blessing in the leadership race and the "Iron Lady" confirmed her support by attending his victory party on Thursday night.
Her backing and the first shadow cabinet appointments have raised questions over Hague's ability to reunite his deeply riven party.
But Parkinson told Channel Four news that Hague's full cabinet would include more moderates.
"If you look at the appointments you will see that William is emphasising that he is determined that all strands of the party should be represented in the shadow cabinet," said Parkinson.
"You've had a very broad spectrum of appointees even in the four we've had and there'll be more that will demonstrate that William is determined to lead a united party."

Parkinson, who is most famous for his resignation in the early 1980s in a blaze of publicity over his affair with his secretary, has been assigned the task of rebuilding support for his diminished party.
Conservative Party membership dwindled during its 18 years in power and the majority of its members are elderly, boding ill for future elections.
Parkinson said his party would emulate the now ruling Labour Party, which finally swept to victory after 18 years in opposition in May after a slick election campaign led by moderniser Tony Blair.
But the party has a tough challenge ahead. It will need an 11 percent swing to win back power from Labour at the next election.
